messages.subject: Re: multipleGroup and Missing Data
messages.subject_clean: multipleGroup and Missing Data
messages.body_plain:
The approach used by 'plausible' is to randomly draw a value from the approximated posterior distribution for each response vector implied by the model. The 'approximate' part is that the posterior is estimated with a Gaussian shape by default, and so a value is sampled according to the EAP and SD(EAP) information given fixed item parameters (more variable plausible scores could be obtained using MCMC to either estimate the individual posteriors more accurately in situations where Guassian approximations are unreasonable, or when you want to include the sampling uncertainty of the item parameter estimates in these plausible values as well). I haven't added full-blown MCMC support to the package yet, but perhaps will sometime in the future.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Identify cases that failed to converge in 'fscores'
messages.body_plain:
Yes, the fscores function has internal components that are returned when cases fail to converge. Specifically, there is an

scores <- fscores(...)
code <- attr(scores,"converge_info_code")
head(code)

where the code vector above contains the convergence code returned by the optimizer (1 = converged, anything else would be non-converged with different flags).

Phil

The levels in the factor()-ization of the object will determine the focal/ref group, as specified in the documentation. If you have supplied a character vector then the function will take group and use

group <- factor(group)

instead, where the first level of this factor is treated as the reference and everything else the focal. If you want a different reference level you should factor() your grouping variable and specify the level ordering manually. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Reduce item levels using GRM item parameters
messages.subject_clean: Reduce item levels using GRM item parameters
messages.body_plain:
Collapsing categories in the context of the GRM will ultimately lead to less information about the measurement of the latent trait, so you could try to justify this perspective from a measurement information context. Personally, I tend to only collapse categories when there is insufficient information available (e.g., like 5 responses for a given Likert scale option) or when the response itself is questionable in the context of measurement (in which case the removal is more diagnostic and justifiable at a theoretical level).

Anytime you change data around there are consequences, with varying intensity, so it would indeed be difficult to find "hard rules" on the topic in the literature (rules of thumb, maybe, though honestly some rules of thumb feel like there's been a carpentry accident on the side of the authors ....).

Phil

Phil

What you've included in the code here is a type of conditional expectation, which could be useful so long as 0,0,0 is a meaningful location to evaluate the behaviour of the latent trait. }
print(a)
d <- rnorm(12, 0, .5)
sigma <- diag(c(1, .5, 1, .5))
dataset <- simdata(a,d,2000,itemtype=rep('2PL', 12),sigma=sigma)

simmod <- bfactor(dataset, specific, model)
coef(simmod, simplify=TRUE)

M2(simmod, QMC=TRUE)

            M2 df       p      RMSEA RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95      SRMSR       TLI       CFI
stats 63.44929 51 0.11325 0.01105047       0 0.01901382 0.02837419 0.9964607 0.9972651
```

I have several questions concerning the item information matrix and selection criteria used in mirt and mirtCAT. These could be elementary questions for somebody here, but I am - as a non-statistician - struggling :-) All the questions are related to a confirmatory multidimensional model with correlated traits, where each item has only one or two non-zero loadings.

First of all, I have a problem conceptually understanding what do the off-diagonal elements of the item information matrix (IIM) represent. Is it un uncertainty related to the difference (or trade-off) between two thetas estimates?

Second, I want to estimate information in the direction of the single dimension. Therefore, the angle between this single direction and my dimension is zero. Thus the weight of a particular element in IIM will be 1 (as the cos(0) = 1 = r). But what about the other dimensions? Will these weights be zero, or should I add the factor correlation? An example: I have two traits correlated r = 0.5. An item has the two factor loadings a_1 = 0.6 and a_2 = 0.7. The item information matrix would be

If I consider the angle 0 and 90 (r = {r_1 = 1, r_2 = 0}), the weighted IIM would be

The latter gives me a sense as off-diagonals are related to discriminations between traits, and therefore, they are not zero. With highly correlated traits, off-diagonals elements will be close to zero, representing the inability to discriminate between correlated dimensions, and vice versa. However, an item could add information even in the factor with zero loading in the latter. Is it correct?

The other question is related to item selection criteria. I did not find any documentation of them, so I ask here:
D-rule (IIM determinant) - this maximalize the ability to estimate each trait and discriminate between them, as it uses the whole information matrix?
T-rule (IIm diagonal) - this maximalize only the ability to estimate each trait, as it does not consider the off-diagonal elements?

W-rule: the same here. What means "the weighted information criteria"? Shouldn't be here a "weighted information matrix"?

Finally, for D-rule, T-rule, and E-rule, it is written "potentially weighted matrix". The matrix is therefore weighted using factors correlation matrix, right?

i would also guess this would happen if no people select certain categories. for example, if for a 7 category item no one selects the lowest category, then it is effectively treated as a 6 category item by mirt and you'll see fewer estimated intercepts than you expect. i don't see any major problem with interpreting the other parameters if this happens, but with a few cautions. if some items have very few people select certain categories, then estimation for some intercepts for that item may be very unstable (look for large-ish standard errors). if you intend to just interpret results for this measurement instrument for a single study, probably fine, but if you wanted to later use such item parameter estimates with a new batch of participants (e.g., for scoring, or a CAT), then it could be problematic (e.g., suppose one of those new participants does select one of the categories that were not selected during calibration).
